column1: Reading|What does literal comprehension primarily involve?|Understanding information explicitly stated in a text|Inventing an unstated event|Ignoring the text|Memorizing only page numbers|Literal questions require locating and interpreting stated information rather than adding assumptions.

Reading|What does inferential comprehension require?|A conclusion supported by textual clues and relevant reasoning|A guess with no evidence|Copying every word|Choosing an answer because it is longest|An inference goes beyond an explicit sentence but must remain supported by evidence and context.

Reading|How does a main idea differ from a supporting detail?|It summarizes the central message supported by the details|It is always the shortest word|It is always the first example|It is every sentence separately|Details develop or support the main idea; a useful summary retains the central message without unnecessary specifics.

Reading|What is skimming mainly used for?|Getting a broad sense of a text quickly|Finding one specific number only|Correcting every comma|Memorizing every sentence|Skimming surveys structure and key ideas; scanning searches for a particular item.

Reading|What is scanning mainly used for?|Locating specific information in a text|Reading every word slowly for all meanings|Writing a poem|Judging a speaker's accent|Scanning targets information such as a date, name or detail using cues from the question.

Reading|Which question encourages critical reading?|What evidence supports the author's claim?|How many letters are in the title?|Can you copy the first sentence?|Which word is printed in the largest font?|Critical reading examines claims, evidence, assumptions and perspectives rather than only surface features.

Reading|What should a reader do when a word has several meanings?|Use its sentence and wider context to choose the relevant meaning|Always choose the first dictionary meaning|Ignore the surrounding sentences|Assume every occurrence has the same meaning|Meaning depends on context; grammar and surrounding ideas help identify the intended sense.

Reading|Why are predictions useful before reading?|They activate prior knowledge and can be checked against the text|They replace reading entirely|They must never be revised|They guarantee the ending|Predictions are tentative; readers should confirm or revise them as evidence appears.

Reading|What is a useful response when comprehension breaks down?|Reread, identify the difficulty and adjust a strategy|Continue mechanically without noticing|Assume the text has no meaning|Memorize random words|Monitoring and repair are part of effective reading; vocabulary, syntax or background knowledge may be the barrier.

Reading|Which activity best checks understanding after reading?|Explain the central idea and cite relevant evidence|Copy the text without explanation|Count all full stops only|Recite the page number|Explanation with evidence demonstrates meaning-making more directly than copying.

Reading|Why should reading materials vary in genre?|Different genres use different purposes, structures and conventions|Only one genre can contain valid information|All texts have identical structures|Genre removes the need for comprehension|Stories, instructions, reports and arguments require different reading strategies and expectations.

Reading|What does reading fluency include?|Accuracy, appropriate pace and expressive phrasing|Only maximum speed|Only loudness|Only memorizing spelling lists|Fluent reading supports meaning; fast word calling without comprehension is insufficient.

Writing|Why is planning useful before writing?|It helps organize purpose, audience and ideas|It guarantees no revision is needed|It makes vocabulary irrelevant|It eliminates the need for sentences|Planning gives direction while leaving room to revise ideas during writing.

Writing|What is the main aim of revising a draft?|Improve ideas, structure and clarity|Only change the paper colour|Only count letters|Only copy the same draft again|Revision considers meaning and organization; proofreading focuses more narrowly on surface errors.

Writing|What is proofreading primarily concerned with?|Checking spelling, punctuation and other surface errors|Replacing all arguments with new research|Choosing an unrelated topic|Ignoring grammar entirely|Proofreading checks the final wording and presentation; major structural changes belong to revision.

Writing|Why should a writing task specify an audience?|Purpose and language choices depend partly on intended readers|Every audience understands the same background|Audience affects only font colour|Readers never influence explanation|Writing for a friend, official or unfamiliar reader calls for different explanations, tone and conventions.

Writing|Which task most clearly gives writing a communicative purpose?|Write instructions another group will use to complete a task|Copy an unrelated paragraph ten times|Write only a date|List random letters|A real reader and purpose let learners check whether their text communicates effectively.

Writing|What is coherence in a paragraph?|Ideas fit together in a logical and meaningful way|Every sentence has exactly the same length|Every word begins with the same letter|Only the handwriting is uniform|Coherence concerns the overall connection of ideas; cohesive devices can help but do not guarantee it.

Writing|What is cohesion in a text?|Language links such as reference words and connectors between parts|Only agreement among readers|Only paper quality|Only the number of pages|Pronouns, repeated key terms and connectors can link sentences, but their use must fit the meaning.

Writing|How should peer feedback on writing be organized?|Use clear criteria and specific respectful suggestions|Only assign personal labels|Avoid reading the draft|Require identical wording in every text|Criteria guide peers toward useful evidence about meaning, organization and language.

Listening and speaking|What is active listening?|Attending to meaning, checking understanding and responding appropriately|Planning only one's own reply without listening|Interrupting every sentence|Judging only the speaker's accent|Active listening involves attention and interpretation, with clarification when needed.

Listening and speaking|Which activity best supports purposeful speaking?|Explain a route so a partner can follow it|Recite random sounds without a goal|Copy a written heading silently|Memorize every classmate's height|A communicative task creates a reason to organize and check the spoken message.

Listening and speaking|Why should a teacher give learners time to formulate an answer?|Processing and language production take time and vary among learners|Silence always means lack of knowledge|Only immediate responses count|Waiting eliminates the need for a question|Wait time can improve participation and the quality of reasoning, especially when language demands are high.

Listening and speaking|What is a suitable use of role-play in language learning?|Practise language for a meaningful social situation|Require disclosure of private personal events|Guarantee every learner has the same personality|Replace every reading activity permanently|Role-play offers supported practice with purpose, audience and context; participation should remain respectful.

Listening and speaking|When can correcting every minor error be counterproductive?|During a fluency-focused exchange where interruptions block communication|During every task without exception|Only when the teacher is absent|When learners have already finished all learning|Feedback should fit the activity. A focused accuracy task and a meaning-focused discussion have different priorities.

Listening and speaking|Which speaking feedback is most useful?|Your explanation is clear; add a landmark so the listener can follow the route|Your accent is unacceptable|Never speak again|You are simply wrong|Specific feedback connects to the communicative goal and gives an actionable improvement.

Language learning|What is a major aim of language pedagogy?|Develop meaningful comprehension and communication|Teach only isolated terminology|Make learners afraid to use language|Eliminate every learner's home language|Grammar and vocabulary support communication, but language education also requires purposeful use and understanding.

Language learning|Why can a learner's home language be a resource?|It supports prior knowledge, identity and connections with new learning|It necessarily prevents all other language learning|It proves low intelligence|It should always be punished|Multilingual resources can bridge concepts and increase participation without ranking languages.

Language learning|What is code-switching in a multilingual context?|Alternating between languages or language varieties in communication|Encrypting every word|Writing only computer code|Replacing every noun with a number|Code-switching can serve communicative functions; its role depends on context and purpose.

Language learning|Why should errors be interpreted during language learning?|They can show developing rules and guide targeted support|They always prove laziness|They mean learning must stop|They make feedback pointless|Error patterns can reveal learners' hypotheses about language, not merely failure to memorize.

Language learning|What is a suitable way to teach vocabulary in context?|Use a meaningful text and compare how the word functions in examples|Teach only an alphabetical list without use|Require one translation for every context|Avoid sentences entirely|Context connects vocabulary with meaning, grammar and use; later practice should support transfer.

Language learning|How can grammar teaching support communication?|Connect forms with meanings and purposes in examples and tasks|Teach rules without any language use|Assume one rule explains every sentence|Avoid feedback on form in every situation|Learners need to see how forms contribute to meaning and then practise using them appropriately.

Language learning|What is a benefit of extensive reading at an appropriate level?|Repeated meaningful exposure to language and ideas|A guarantee that no vocabulary support is needed|A substitute for all writing|An obligation to read only the most difficult texts|Sustained accessible reading can build fluency and vocabulary; suitability and interest matter.

Language learning|What is a benefit of intensive reading?|Close analysis of a selected text for specific learning purposes|Reading without attention to meaning|Counting books without opening them|Using only pictures without discussion|Intensive reading focuses carefully on a short text's meaning, language or organization.

Language learning|Why should language teaching integrate skills when suitable?|Real communication often combines listening, speaking, reading and writing|Every skill is exactly identical|Integration makes goals unnecessary|A learner must master every skill before attempting any task|Integrated tasks can connect skills, while focused practice remains useful for particular difficulties.

Assessment|Which assessment is most aligned with an oral communication goal?|Observe a relevant speaking task using clear criteria|Use only a spelling dictation|Use only attendance|Use only handwriting speed|Assessment should elicit the intended capability; speaking requires evidence from speaking.

Assessment|Which assessment best checks inferential reading?|Ask for a supported conclusion and the clues behind it|Ask only for the page number|Require copying the title|Test only the meaning of punctuation marks|Inference requires connecting clues; an explanation reveals whether the conclusion is supported.

Assessment|What is a useful purpose of a language portfolio?|Show work, revision and reflection over time|Store only unrelated certificates|Hide every early draft|Replace all feedback with a cover design|A portfolio can document development when selection and reflection are purposeful and criteria are clear.

Assessment|Why should a teacher distinguish language difficulty from subject understanding?|A learner may understand a concept but struggle to express it in the assessment language|Language never affects performance|Every wrong answer is a conceptual failure|All learners have identical vocabulary|Language demands can be an access barrier; varied representations and dialogue can help locate the difficulty.

Assessment|What is constructive self-assessment in language learning?|Use criteria to identify strengths, difficulties and next steps|Give oneself a perfect score without evidence|Compare only with a classmate's handwriting|Ignore all feedback|Self-assessment develops monitoring when learners understand goals and use evidence from their own work.

Remediation|A learner retrieves facts but struggles with inference. What is targeted support?|Practise linking a conclusion to specific textual clues|Repeat only spelling lists|Remove all reading tasks|Require copying longer passages|The identified gap is inferential reasoning, so practice should connect evidence with conclusions.

Remediation|A learner writes sentence fragments. What is targeted support?|Compare complete and incomplete sentences and revise a short draft|Practise only faster handwriting|Memorize map symbols|Read only chapter titles|Teaching should address sentence completeness with examples and revision rather than an unrelated skill.

Remediation|A learner knows words individually but cannot understand a complex sentence. What should be examined?|Relationships among clauses, reference words and sentence structure|Only notebook colour|Only the learner's age|Only alphabetical order|Comprehension can break down at syntactic relationships even when individual vocabulary is familiar.

Remediation|Why should later tasks check transfer after remedial teaching?|Success on the identical exercise may not show understanding in a new context|One repeated answer proves every future task is mastered|Transfer is unrelated to language|Only the total number of worksheets matters|New relevant examples help show whether the learner can apply a strategy beyond the practised item.

Materials|What makes a passage appropriate for a learning task?|Its language, content, accessibility and purpose fit the learners and goal|It is always the longest available passage|It contains the most rare words|It excludes every familiar experience|Appropriateness depends on learning demands, prior knowledge and access, not length or difficulty alone.

Materials|How can pictures support a language task?|Provide context for description, sequencing or inference|Replace every need for language use|Guarantee only one interpretation in every case|Make evidence irrelevant|Images can stimulate meaningful communication when questions and purposes are clear.

Materials|Why can authentic notices or instructions be useful?|They show language serving a real communicative purpose|They always require no adaptation|They are automatically suitable for every age|They contain no conventions|Authentic materials illustrate use, but teachers should consider complexity, accessibility and context.

Materials|What is an appropriate use of a multilingual glossary?|Support comprehension while retaining meaningful language use|Require word-for-word translation of every text|Replace every discussion|Define one language as superior|A glossary can bridge unfamiliar vocabulary; comprehension still depends on context and relationships.

Exam preparation|What should a candidate confirm before choosing Language I and Language II?|Permitted languages and the requirement that the choices differ where specified|Only the website's default display language|Only the candidate's handwriting style|Only the colour of the admit card|The official bulletin defines examination language choices. Website display language does not select the official exam languages.

Exam preparation|Do generic language-teaching questions replace all language-specific comprehension practice?|No; chosen languages require their own texts and language-specific practice|Yes; one pedagogy definition covers every reading task|Yes; grammar and comprehension are unnecessary|Yes; display-language buttons are sufficient|Shared pedagogy foundations are useful, but complete preparation also requires content for the actual chosen languages.
